name: Abdominal organs and vessels
summary: The organs of a female abdomen in their natural positions, with the heart, trachea and oesophagus above: digestive tract, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, suprarenal glands, ureters, bladder, uterus and ovaries. The aorta and its gut branches are red; the venae cavae and the portal venous system are blue. Made for an e-learning module on examining the abdomen.
clinical: When flow through the liver is obstructed (most often by cirrhosis), pressure in the portal vein rises. Blood reroutes through portosystemic anastomoses, which causes oesophageal varices, caput medusae and rectal varices, and the spleen enlarges.

The abdominal aorta descends just left of the midline and divides into the common iliac arteries at about L4, roughly the level of the umbilicus. An aneurysm shows as a pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus, and rupture presents with abdominal or back pain and shock.

Heart.name: Heart
Heart.description: The heart lies in the middle mediastinum and rests on the diaphragm, directly above the liver and stomach. This model shows it in one piece with the roots of the great vessels. Its apex is normally in the left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

Trachea.name: Trachea
Trachea.description: The windpipe runs from the cricoid cartilage (C6) to its bifurcation into the main bronchi at about T4/T5, the level of the sternal angle. It lies directly in front of the oesophagus.

Cartilage trachea.name: Tracheal cartilages
Cartilage trachea.description: C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that keep the trachea open. They are open at the back, where the trachealis muscle bridges the gap next to the oesophagus.

Cartilage throat.name: Laryngeal cartilages
Cartilage throat.description: The thyroid and cricoid cartilages of the larynx, at the top of the trachea. The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple). The cricothyroid membrane between the two is the site of an emergency cricothyroidotomy.

Artery 1.name: Aorta
Artery 1.description: The aortic arch, descending thoracic aorta and abdominal aorta, which divides at about L4 into the common iliac arteries. Small renal arteries branch off to the kidneys. In this model, red means arteries.

Artery 2.name: Coeliac trunk branches
Artery 2.description: Foregut arteries from the coeliac trunk (T12). The gastric arteries run along the lesser curvature of the stomach, the gastro-omental arcade runs along the greater curvature, and the hepatic artery heads towards the liver.

Artery 3.name: Superior mesenteric artery branches
Artery 3.description: The superior mesenteric artery leaves the aorta at L1, behind the neck of the pancreas, and supplies the midgut through its jejunal, ileal, ileocolic and colic branches. The midgut runs from the middle of the duodenum to the distal third of the transverse colon. The branches are linked by arcades in the mesentery.

Vein 1.name: Venae cavae
Vein 1.description: The superior vena cava drains the upper body into the right atrium. The inferior vena cava ascends to the right of the aorta and collects the common iliac and renal veins, plus smaller tributaries. The left renal vein is longer because it crosses in front of the aorta. In this model, blue means veins.

Vein 2.name: Hepatic portal vein and tributaries
Vein 2.description: The superior mesenteric and splenic veins join behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein. It carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut, pancreas and spleen to the liver, rather than to the heart.

Vein 3.name: Intrahepatic portal vein branches
Vein 3.description: The portal vein divides into right and left branches at the porta hepatis and keeps branching inside the liver. Its blood ends in the hepatic sinusoids, which drain through the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava.

Intestine Small Dunne darms.name: Oesophagus, stomach and small intestine
Intestine Small Dunne darms.description: One continuous part in this model. The oesophagus runs down behind the heart to the stomach in the left upper quadrant, which empties into the duodenum, jejunum and ileum. The small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption, and the ileum ends at the ileocaecal valve.

Intestine Large Dikke darms.name: Large intestine
Intestine Large Dikke darms.description: The large intestine runs from the caecum in the right iliac fossa through the ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon to the rectum, framing the loops of small intestine. It absorbs water and electrolytes. The ascending and descending colon are retroperitoneal, while the transverse and sigmoid colon hang on a mesentery.

Lever.name: Liver
Lever.description: The largest gland in the body. It fills the right upper quadrant under the diaphragm and is shown translucent here so the vessels inside it are visible. About three quarters of its blood comes through the portal vein and the rest through the hepatic artery.

Gallbladder Galblaas.name: Gallbladder
Gallbladder Galblaas.description: A pear-shaped sac on the underside of the liver, shown with its duct, that stores and concentrates bile. Its fundus sits at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage. An inflamed gallbladder causes right upper quadrant pain (Murphy's sign).

Pancreas.name: Pancreas
Pancreas.description: A retroperitoneal gland behind the stomach. Its head sits in the C-loop of the duodenum and its tail reaches the hilum of the spleen. It has an exocrine role (digestive enzymes) and an endocrine role (insulin and glucagon from the islets).

Spleen Milt.name: Spleen
Spleen Milt.description: A lymphoid organ in the left upper quadrant under ribs 9 to 11, behind the stomach. It filters old red blood cells and blood-borne pathogens. It is often injured in blunt trauma, especially with left lower rib fractures.

Kidney R.name: Right kidney
Kidney R.description: A retroperitoneal organ on the posterior abdominal wall. It usually sits slightly lower than the left kidney because the liver lies above it.

Kidney L.name: Left kidney
Kidney L.description: A retroperitoneal organ on the posterior abdominal wall, lying behind the stomach, pancreas and descending colon, with the spleen above and lateral to it. Its renal vein crosses in front of the aorta to reach the inferior vena cava.

Suprarenal R.name: Right suprarenal gland
Suprarenal R.description: A pyramid-shaped endocrine gland capping the upper pole of the right kidney. The cortex makes corticosteroids (cortisol and aldosterone) and the medulla makes adrenaline.

Suprarenal L.name: Left suprarenal gland
Suprarenal L.description: A crescent-shaped endocrine gland on the upper, medial border of the left kidney. The cortex makes corticosteroids and the medulla makes adrenaline and noradrenaline.

Urether R1.name: Right ureter
Urether R1.description: A muscular tube that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. It runs down on the psoas muscle and crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery. Stones tend to lodge at the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the entry to the bladder.

Urether L.name: Left ureter
Urether L.description: A muscular tube that carries urine from the left renal pelvis to the bladder. It runs down on the psoas muscle and crosses the pelvic brim near the bifurcation of the common iliac artery.

Bladder Blaas.name: Urinary bladder
Bladder Blaas.description: A hollow muscular reservoir behind the pubic symphysis. In the female, as here, the uterus lies over its posterosuperior surface. When full, it rises above the pubis and can be felt or percussed in the suprapubic region.

Uterus1.name: Uterus and uterine tubes
Uterus1.description: The uterus usually lies anteverted and anteflexed over the bladder. The uterine (Fallopian) tubes run laterally from its upper corners and open near the ovaries with fringe-like fimbriae. Fertilisation normally takes place in the ampulla of the tube.

Ovary L.name: Left ovary
Ovary L.description: The female gonad, lying in the ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall. It produces oocytes, oestrogen and progesterone. It is supplied by the ovarian artery, which comes straight from the abdominal aorta.

Ovary R.name: Right ovary
Ovary R.description: The female gonad, lying in the ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall. It produces oocytes and sex hormones, and its blood supply comes directly from the aorta through the ovarian artery.

Ovary Ligament L.name: Ligament of ovary
Ovary Ligament L.description: A fibrous cord joining the ovary to the uterus just below the uterine tube. With the round ligament of the uterus, it is a remnant of the gubernaculum.

Ovary Ligament R.name: Ligament of ovary
Ovary Ligament R.description: A fibrous cord joining the ovary to the uterus just below the uterine tube. With the round ligament of the uterus, it is a remnant of the gubernaculum.

notes: Labels = Dutch text-label cards (Lever, Maag, Nier, Bijnier, Colon..., Rectum), dropped. 'Intestine Small Dunne darms' is one mesh (stomach material) that also contains the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum, so it cannot be split; named for all three. Vein 1: the SVC/IVC, common iliac and renal veins are certain. It also has several thin branches (towards the liver, one reaching towards the spleen, and a thin vessel running up behind on the left, possibly azygos/hemi-azygos) that I could not identify confidently, so they are not named. Vein 3 is taken as intrahepatic portal branches because it starts where the portal vein trunk (Vein 2) ends; it could alternatively depict hepatic veins. Artery 2 = arcades on the stomach plus a branch to the liver; the coeliac trunk origin itself was not clearly visible. The uterus, ovary and ligament of ovary do not resolve in the (male) atlas, so their structures are empty.
